bullets: The new ChartAct release tests dynamic chart understanding through real browser interactions. Models and graphical user interface agents must hover, click, zoom, drag, scroll, and select controls to answer questions, rather than interpret only static chart images. Why it matters: If you are choosing an evaluation for chart assistants or browser agents, ChartAct can reveal whether a model can obtain information hidden behind interactive controls—behavior that a static visual-question benchmark cannot measure. Evidence: E001. High confidence.

The new LongHaul-Bench release evaluates a self-improving agent across roughly 1,000 sequential episodes while preserving its evolving knowledge state and enforcing a fixed experience-memory budget. It compares this agent with a frozen control across five reproducibly generated industrial environments. Why it matters: If you are testing agents that learn after deployment, this design shifts the decision from one-session task accuracy to whether accumulated experience improves or degrades reliability over time under deployment constraints. Evidence: E028. High confidence.

The newly released permission-withdrawal study evaluates tool-using agents at the action-trajectory level: whether an unauthorized operation was proposed, approved, dispatched, or blocked after a user narrowed permissions. Final-state scoring alone cannot distinguish those paths. Why it matters: If you are selecting a safety test for tool-using agents, this means a harmless final state is insufficient evidence of compliance; the evaluation must inspect intermediate authorization decisions and recovery behavior. Evidence: E036. High confidence.

The newly released functional near-infrared spectroscopy study makes evaluation leakage—the accidental use of test information during model correction—a measured variable. It compares semi-nested evaluation with fully nested cross-validation, boundary separation, null tests, and a second cohort. Separate captured artifacts also package leakage-aware protocols for photovoltaic diagnosis and intrusion detection. Why it matters: If you compare predictive systems built from grouped, temporal, or repeatedly processed observations, these releases support choosing suites that isolate every learned correction inside the training split; otherwise, reported gains may reflect information crossing the test boundary. Evidence: E027, E098, E017. High confidence.

The new GraphIV benchmark release changes research-agent retrieval from finding one matching paper to recovering a complementary cohort of papers cited by arXiv review articles. It includes three benchmarks built around those review cohorts. Why it matters: If you are evaluating automated literature research, this design tests whether a retriever assembles enough distinct evidence to answer a broad question, rather than rewarding a single superficially relevant hit. Evidence: E016. Medium confidence.

The new Prompt Accessibility Controlled Evaluation testbed evaluates accessibility in large-language-model-generated HyperText Markup Language form components under controlled prompt conditions. It covers 58 components from five developer-focused models and varies system prompts with increasing accessibility guidance. Why it matters: If you are comparing coding models for interface generation, the controlled prompt changes help separate model behavior from instruction quality and support a more specific product decision than scoring complete webpages with loosely matched tasks. Evidence: E018. Medium confidence.
bullets_zh: 新版 ChartAct 通过真实的浏览器交互测试动态图表理解能力。模型和图形用户界面智能体必须通过悬停、点击、缩放、拖动、滚动和选择控件来回答问题，而不是只解读静态图表图像。Why it matters: 如果你正在为图表助手或浏览器智能体选择评测，ChartAct 可以揭示模型能否获取隐藏在交互式控件背后的信息——这是静态视觉问答基准无法衡量的行为。Evidence: E001. High confidence.

新版 LongHaul-Bench 在大约 1,000 个连续回合中评估一个自我改进的智能体，同时保留其持续演化的知识状态，并实施固定的经验记忆预算。它在 five 个可复现生成的工业环境中，将该智能体与冻结的对照智能体进行比较。Why it matters: 如果你正在测试部署后继续学习的智能体，这一设计会将决策重点从单次会话的任务准确率，转向在部署约束下，累积经验是否会随时间推移改善或削弱可靠性。Evidence: E028. High confidence.
新发布的权限撤回研究在动作轨迹层面评估工具使用型智能体：在用户收窄权限后，未经授权的操作是被提出、批准、下发还是拦截。仅对最终状态评分无法区分这些路径。Why it matters: 如果你正在为工具使用型智能体选择安全测试，这意味着无害的最终状态并不足以证明其合规；评测必须检查中间授权决策和恢复行为。Evidence: E036. High confidence.

新发布的功能性近红外光谱研究将评测泄漏——模型校正过程中意外使用测试信息——设为一个被测变量。它比较了半嵌套评测与完全嵌套交叉验证、边界分离、零假设检验以及另一队列。另行收录的产物还为光伏诊断和入侵检测提供了具备泄漏意识的协议。Why it matters: 如果你要比较基于分组、时序或经过重复处理的观测数据构建的预测系统，这些发布成果支持选择能将每项学习得到的校正严格限制在训练集内部的评测套件；否则，报告中的性能提升可能反映的是信息跨越了测试边界。Evidence: E027, E098, E017. High confidence.

新版 GraphIV 基准将研究智能体的检索任务从寻找一篇匹配论文，转变为找回由 arXiv 综述文章引用、彼此互补的一组论文。它包含围绕这些综述论文群组构建的 three 项基准。Why it matters: 如果你正在评估自动化文献研究，这一设计测试的是检索器能否汇集足够多样的证据来回答宽泛问题，而不是奖励单个表面相关的检索结果。Evidence: E016. Medium confidence.

新版 Prompt Accessibility Controlled Evaluation 测试平台在受控提示条件下，评估大语言模型生成的 HyperText Markup Language 表单组件的无障碍性。它涵盖来自 five 个面向开发者的模型的 58 个组件，并使用逐步增加无障碍指导的系统提示。Why it matters: 如果你正在比较用于界面生成的编程模型，受控的提示变化有助于区分模型行为与指令质量，并且相比对任务匹配较为宽松的完整网页进行评分，能够支持更具体的产品决策。Evidence: E018. Medium confidence.

evidence_items.summary: A synthetic dataset of 500 long multi-turn Arabic conversations with a mean conversation length of 33.056 turns, median of 33 turns, range of 24–48 turns, and a total of 16,528 turns (where every turn is one user message together with its expected agent response). Conversation length in tokens has a mean of 9,901, a median of 11,060, and a range of 710–18,456. Token counts cover the user side of each conversation and are computed under the cl100k base tokenizer, since the dataset specifies an expected response for each turn rather than a fixed agent reply. The dataset is not partitioned. It is intended for evaluation rather than training, so all 500 conversations form a single test set. Each conversation follows one of five composition templates, allocated in equal proportion at 100 conversations each, combining personal information about a fictional persona with excerpts from Arabic Wikipedia articles and short general-knowledge exchanges. Every turn is annotated with the memory-dependent design objectives it probes, an English description of its role in the conversation, and the expected response. Across the dataset this yields 22,214 objective instances over ten design objectives, of which 16,310 query information established earlier in the same conversation. The number of turns separating a queried fact from its introduction has a median of 15 and a maximum of 47. The generation process drew on 1,200 Arabic Wikipedia articles spanning thirteen categories and totalling 4,649,321 words, with each article used in exactly one conversation, and on a curated pool of 1,244 Arabic general-knowledge topics across seventeen categories. Conversations were produced with Gemma 3 (12B) under a fixed random seed, from a plan computed deterministically in advance.

evidence_items.summary: YemSarc is the first multimodal (text, audio, and video) benchmark dataset for sarcasm detection in Yemeni dialectal Arabic and seven additional Arabic dialects. It comprises 630 balanced utterances (315 sarcastic, 315 non-sarcastic) drawn from naturally occurring conversational exchanges across eight Arabic dialects: Mahwiti, Ibbi, Adeni, Sanaani, Dhamari, Saudi, Egyptian, and Taizzi. Each target utterance is paired with its preceding conversational context and is represented across three synchronized modalities: written transcript, audio segment, and video frame sequence. The dataset was constructed from two widely popular Yemeni comedic drama series (Bayt Al-Madaliz and Khuruj Nihai), sourced from their official YouTube channels. Annotation was carried out through a structured three-phase protocol by three expert academic linguists, achieving a final inter-annotator agreement of Fleiss' Kappa = 0.7473. The dataset is released with a fully reproducible, speaker-independent, and statistically audited evaluation pipeline. This dataset is intended for non-commercial academic research purposes, including multimodal sarcasm detection, Arabic dialectal NLP, and social media analysis. The dataset is licensed under CC BY 4.0.
evidence_items.title: YemSarc: A Multimodal Benchmark Dataset for Sarcasm Detection in Yemeni and Related Arabic Dialects

evidence_items.summary: NeuralSpeed: An Infrastructure-Level Approach to Efficient Large Language Model Inference Abstract The growing adoption of large language models (LLMs) in enterprise applications, automated workflows, and multi-agent systems has increased the importance of inference efficiency, response latency, and infrastructure utilization. NeuralSpeed is an AI infrastructure technology designed to improve the efficiency of LLM-powered applications while maintaining compatibility with established deployment environments. The project investigates methods for improving inference efficiency in multi-interaction workloads, with an emphasis on operational performance, response consistency, and integration flexibility. The technology is designed to operate at the infrastructure level, reducing the need for changes to existing application architectures or underlying model parameters. Its development focuses on the following objectives: Inference efficiency: Improving the utilization of computational resources in supported workloads. Operational performance: Reducing unnecessary processing overhead where technically feasible. Integration flexibility: Supporting integration into existing AI application environments. Response integrity: Maintaining appropriate output structure and application-level compatibility. Deployment practicality: Evaluating performance under representative operational conditions. Initial evaluations indicate potential performance and efficiency benefits in selected workloads. Results depend on the workload, model, provider, configuration, and evaluation methodology. Further validation is required to establish generalizability across different deployment environments. Technical Scope NeuralSpeed is an infrastructure-oriented research and development project focused on the operational efficiency of LLM-based systems. This publication presents the project's general objectives, intended application domain, and high-level evaluation scope.

evidence_items.summary: This dataset provides a reproducible benchmark for evaluating lexical retrieval from OCR/HTR transcriptions of postwar Japanese student and social movement materials. Version 1.0.0 contains a 106-page reference corpus, 69 exact-match queries, 475 positive query-page relevance judgments, page-level recognition outputs for 12 experimental conditions, and a standalone Python script reproducing the Stage 3 retrieval metrics. The benchmark was initially developed for the JINMONCOM 2026 study and can also serve as a common evaluation basis for subsequent OCR/HTR research. The reference transcriptions follow the upstream dataset v1.1.0 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21798820), and trained OCR/HTR models are separately available (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23291038). This release preserves the fixed evaluation data used in the original study without revising the underlying transcriptions. Future releases may extend the evaluation conditions or benchmark data, with changes documented separately for reproducibility.

evidence_items.summary: Digital health systems have faced persistent challenges in predictive reliability, data integrity, and secure interoperability across distributed stakeholders. Conventional machine learning models have relied on centralized data repositories, which have limited trust, auditability, and longitudinal consistency. Graph-theoretical approaches have emerged as promising tools for modeling complex health interactions, while blockchain architecture has ensured immutability and decentralized trust. However, its combined application for health prediction has remained underexplored. Conventional digital health prediction frameworks have lacked a unified mechanism that captures the relational dependencies among patients, symptoms, and clinical outcomes while simultaneously guaranteeing secure data provenance. Most of the graph-based models have ignored trust management, and most of the blockchain-based systems have underutilized structural intelligence, which has resulted in fragmented and inefficient predictive pipelines. This study has proposed a novel graph-theoretic algorithm named Adaptive Health Influence Graph Traversal (AHIGT), which has modeled patient-centric health events as weighted temporal graphs. The algorithm has computed predictive risk scores through an influence propagation that has adapted to the dynamic edge relevance. A permissioned blockchain layer has been combined to store graph updates, model parameters, and prediction hashes, which has ensured transparency and tamper resistance. Smart contracts have governed data access and model update validation, which has preserved privacy while enabling collaborative learning. Experimental evaluation on benchmark digital health datasets has shown that the proposed AHIGT framework has achieved improved predictive performance with a maximum accuracy of 0.85, precision of 0.84, recall of 0.83, and an F1-score of 0.84 compared with conventional graph-based methods. Computation time per patient remains efficient at 1.05 seconds, which shows scalability for real-time deployment. The addition of adaptive graph traversal with a blockchain has allowed data integrity, auditability, and collaborative updates, confirming the robustness and reliability of the predictive framework under dynamic and multi-source health data conditions.
evidence_items.title: Enhancing Predictive Digital Health Analytics Using Blockchain-Based Graph Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: PGMem is a Python implementation of a provenance-governed framework for an agentic personal assistant. The assistant is designed for people with mild cognitive impairment, mild dementia or acquired brain injury. The package implements: an evidence-typed personal event base; graduated assistance with permission-gated escalation; threshold-based grounded recall with abstention; consent checks at execution time; the framework's four operating invariants. Nineteen automated tests check the code against the paper's equations, invariants and counterexamples. A synthetic dataset accompanies the code. It contains 240 participants, 17,142 task episodes, 3,081 records and 4,320 recall questions, described by Frictionless Data Package metadata. The metadata supports cohort statistics and validation of real datasets with the same structure. Compared with a reminder app and a single-agent RAG baseline on identical histories, the framework showed: zero invented outcomes and zero fabricated recollections; zero contacts with a trusted person after consent was withdrawn; the lowest false-prompt rate (0.20). In exchange, task success (0.82 vs 0.91) and answer coverage (0.62) were lower. All data are synthetic, so the results illustrate how the rules behave and do not show clinical benefit.
evidence_items.title: PGMem: A Reference Implementation of Provenance-Governed Agentic Memory Support with a Synthetic Dataset and Statistical Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence is now used to evaluate other systems. Large language models (LLMs) generate assurance profiles, control questions and test cases, judge benchmark outputs, and support automated red teams. At the same time, the evaluated systems are often LLM-based agents themselves. In this position paper, we argue that this situation creates a new type of assurance problem. Three basic assumptions of classical evaluation are broken: (1) the evaluator and the target can fail in the same way (correlated blind spots); (2) the evaluation criteria are written by the same type of model that is evaluated (circular criteria); and (3) the target can influence the inputs of the evaluator (injectable evaluation). We connect this problem to known results in computer science and propose seven principles for what we call metaassurance. Finally, we present four testable propositions for future research.
evidence_items.title: WHO ASSURES THE ASSURER? A POSITION ON META-ASSURANCE FOR AI-MEDIATED EVALUATION

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are used to generate user interface (UI) code, yet the accessibility of this code is difficult to evaluate in a controlled way. Existing evaluations typically examine full-generated webpages or loosely specified tasks, which makes it difficult to determine where accessibility outcomes come from. We introduce PACE for “Prompt Accessibility Controlled Evaluation,” a benchmarking testbed for controlled evaluation of accessibility in LLM-generated HTML form components. Using PACE, we evaluated the accessibility of 58 form components generated by five developer-centric LLMs with variations across three system prompts with increasing accessibility guidance, and three request variants containing increasing detail about each form components. We collected 10 trials per configuration for a total of n = 26, 100 outputs. Our findings show that accessibility in LLM-generated code moved with prompt construction and with the circumstance around it (e.g., model, form component, and measure used to assess the output). This pattern calls for evaluation designs that can better separate sources of variation in the accessibility of LLM-generated code.
evidence_items.title: Prompt and Circumstance: Evaluating Accessibility in LLM-Generated HTML Form Components

evidence_items.summary: As AI becomes embedded in accessibility research, critical questions arise about representation, participation, and power. This focused critical review examines 26 papers presenting empirical, user-facing AI-based interactive systems involving people with disabilities, drawn from the ACM Digital Library (2019–2026). The corpus is dominated by work with people who are blind or have low vision and by generative AI approaches such as large language models and diffusion models; several disability communities remain sparsely represented. People with disabilities participated most consistently in evaluation, while earlier involvement in problem framing was rare. Most papers acknowledged ethical concerns only in passing; few treated them as structuring design constraints.
evidence_items.title: Representation, Participation, and Power in AI-Based Interactive Systems for Accessibility: A Critical Review

evidence_items.summary: Zero-trust security requires continuous identity verification, but repeated re-authentication creates friction that users work around. This thesis investigates whether keyboard and mouse dynamics can support continuous authentication across three datasets: a primary collection of approximately 30 users (Dataset A), the KMT benchmark of 88 users (Dataset B), and a multi-session dataset of 8 users with 6 to 9 sessions each (Dataset C). The core contribution is mode-aware fusion, which retains single-modality windows rather than discarding any window missing either keyboard or mouse activity. On Dataset C, this recovers 44.5% of usable windows that an inner-join pipeline would drop and keeps three of eight users in scope who would otherwise be unmodeled. Mouse-only authentication on recovered windows reaches EER 0.030 on the strongest user, while keyboard-only authentication fails for six of eight users due to insufficient activity or the limits of character-agnostic free-text features. Cross-dataset transfer between Datasets A and B failed, indicating that per-deployment enrollment is required in production. The system is positioned as a soft signal within a layered zero-trust architecture, not a standalone gate.
evidence_items.title: Multimodal Behavioral Biometrics for Continuous Authentication in Zero-Trust Systems: A Multi-Dataset Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Machine-learning research on water cyber-physical systems (CPS) is constrained by datasets that are either real but chemicallypoor, or simulated but free of sensing noise and attacks. We present AquaSense-ICS, an open dataset and benchmark that co-registers (i) a 25.4 h recording window (8.0 h of recorded data, 26% coverage) from a Raspberry Pi 5 edge node (TDS probe andBME680 ambient sensor, 1–2 s sampling, 23,688 records), with (ii) a looped network of 13 nodes (10 junctions, 2 reservoirs, 1tank) simulated in EPANET-MSX for six water-quality species, (iii) a parameterised library of cyber-attacks (false data injection,replay, denial of service, drift) and unintentional sensor faults with sample-level ground truth, and (iv) augmented and TimeGAN-generated sequences, flagged by an origin column. The attack, fault and water-quality labels are traceable to a seeded generator,a documented rule or a simulation input. We show that the most common way of benchmarking such hybrid data, random rowsplits and labels computed from the input features, yields near-perfect but uninformative scores (macro-F1 = 0.9998 for RandomForest), and we replace it with a leakage-aware protocol using chronological splits and held-out attack types rather than labelreconstruction. Under this protocol, no model exceeds the constant “normal” predictor for attack classification (macro-F1 = 0.465),and the best detectors reach a mean AUROC of 0.64 on attack types unseen during training (0.35–0.93 depending on the type),leaving substantial headroom. Data and simulation files are released under CC BY 4.0 at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23390541, and attack generators and benchmark code under MIT.
evidence_items.title: AquaSense-ICS: A Hybrid Real-Simulated Cyber-Physical Dataset and Leakage-Aware Benchmark for Smart Water Quality Monitoring and Attack Detection

evidence_items.summary: Background Image-based dietary assessment is useful for precision diabetes care. Multimodal Large Language Models (mLLMs) may greatly facilitate dietary self-monitoring. However, comprehensive evaluation of their real-world accuracy remains limited. Methods We developed SeeFood, an open-source benchmark, and evaluated eight commercial and open-source mLLMs on 80 real-world meal photographs from the SNAPMe dataset for nutrient and energy estimation (calories, carbohydrates, protein, fat, fiber), food-item identification, and day-level diet quality (Healthy Eating Index, HEI-2020). Three finalists were evaluated on the complete dataset (1680 photographs, 275 participant-days), and the best model was analyzed by meal type, portion size, sizing-marker use, ingredient visibility and meal complexity. Results GPT-4o mini achieved the lowest errors, with a significant advantage for carbohydrates; the three finalists performed similarly on other outcomes and on HEI-2020. Mean absolute percentage errors (MAPE) remained high (52%--90%), and the direction of bias was model-specific. The carbohydrate mean absolute error was 13.3 g (95% CI 12.4--14.3), and only 57% of meals were within +/- 10 g, a clinically relevant threshold for insulin dosing in type 1 diabetes. Calorie errors for lunch and dinner were in the range reported for human estimation on other images (~55% MAPE), whereas drink-only images had the highest relative errors (312% MAPE) because of dissolved sugars. Food items were reliably identified when fully visible (Dice = 0.74), and HEI-2020 estimates showed moderate agreement with reference values (RMSE = 12.5 points; r = 0.61). Larger portions were increasingly underestimated, and sizing references did not improve accuracy. Newer or larger models and chain-of-thought prompting did not consistently improve performance.
evidence_items.title: Image-Based Dietary Assessment Using Multimodal Large Language Models: Performance, Limitations, and Clinical Applicability in Diabetes

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT The rapid advancement of Generative AI (GenAI) creates new opportunities for spatial planning. However, most existing applications focus on macro‐scale overhead perspectives, leaving street‐level visualization constrained by strict physical and spatial fidelity challenges. We introduce a controllable GenAI‐human interactive framework for producing spatially faithful and realistic street‐level imagery that reflects envisioned planning scenarios. Using Large‐scale solar photovoltaic (LSPV) site planning as a test case, it leverages vision‐language models to integrate human inputs (e.g., textual intent, scribbles) and existing status photos, synthesizing photorealistic outcomes. To support systematic evaluation, we constructed a large‐scale street‐view imagery dataset of before‐and‐after solar panel installation across the United States. We comprehensively evaluated 11 model settings covering five open‐sourced diffusion models and one commercial vision foundation model to test fidelity and realism. Our study illustrates how a GenAI‐human interactive pipeline can support visualizing proposed environmental interventions, and offers a benchmark for conditioned GenAI visualization applications.
evidence_items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence for Planning Scenario Visualization: A Framework and Benchmark for Controllable Street‐Level Image Synthesis

evidence_items.summary: Self-improving agents built on large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for industrial fault diagnosis, but it is not known whether the experience such an agent accumulates over months of operation makes it more reliable or slowly corrupts it, least of all under edge-deployment constraints. We present LongHaul-Bench, a seed-reproducible synthetic industrial environment and protocol that follows an agent's knowledge state over about 1,000 sequential episodes with a quantized 3B-parameter model and a hard experience-memory budget. Across five independently generated worlds, experiential learning lifts exact accuracy over a frozen control by 3.8 points (complete rank separation; Holm-corrected p = .048). Plausibly corrupted feedback induces dose-dependent knowledge rot (-6.0 points at 40% corruption; -2.3, not significant, at 20%), whereas blatantly invalid feedback is inert. We explain these effects with a recall-precision decomposition computed on episode-matched pairs: memory adds about 9 points when a recall surfaces the correct precedent and removes about 20 points when it misleads, so memory helps only above a break-even recall precision of roughly 0.7. Plausible corruption leaves the cost of a misleading recall unchanged and instead lowers recall precision (0.81, 0.72, 0.65 at 0/20/40%); the precision drop alone accounts for the full loss at 20% and three-quarters of it at 40%. LLM-free manual-consistency gates recover the damage by restoring precision to 0.78, yet suppress two-thirds of memory's benefit when manuals are incomplete, and memory's value is an order of magnitude larger for a weaker 3B model family (+28 vs. +2.3 points). Generator, harness, run logs, and analysis scripts are released at https://github.com/vahit19/longhaul-bench.
evidence_items.title: LongHaul-Bench: A Reproducible Benchmark for Long-Horizon Reliability of Self-Improving LLM Agents Under Industrial Edge Constraints

evidence_items.summary: This is a minor release. Its highlight is the support for repeated measures in the evaluation module, for validation studies that record several nights per participant. It also adds a new method to compare detected events based on their overlap and fixes a deprecation warning with pandas 3.1. Evaluation module: support several nights per subject (repeated measures) yasa.EpochByEpochAgreement and yasa.SleepStatsAgreement accept a new subjects argument that tells YASA which participant each night belongs to. The nights of a participant are not independent, and treating them as such makes the confidence intervals and p-values too small. With subjects , both classes account for the clustering of nights within participants, following Bland & Altman (2007) , Zou (2013) and Parker et al. (2016) . With one night per participant, the results are unchanged. See the new Several nights per subject section of the evaluation tutorial. (#279) Improvements yasa.compare detection and the compare channels and compare detection methods of the detection results accept method="intersection" to match events based on the overlap of their intervals (intersection over union) instead of the distance between their onsets. This makes it possible to compare detections with different sampling frequencies, and prevents split, merged or duplicate detections from all counting as true positives. The default method="distance" is unchanged. (#88, #278) compare channels is up to 6 times faster, as the events of each channel are now validated and sorted once and each pair of channels is compared once. (#282) Bugfixes Fixed a Pandas4Warning in yasa.SleepStaging with pandas 3.1, which deprecates the inplace keyword of sort index . (#283) Dependencies statsmodels is a new optional dependency, required only for the mixed models of yasa.SleepStatsAgreement with several nights per participant. Install it with pip install yasa[stats] (included in yasa[full] ).

evidence_items.summary: Two changes to fits, under "Changed": magnitude slots="auto" , 10 beam slots for regression, and a guard in the search against quotients whose denominator comes near zero. With magnitude slots=0 a fit gives 0.6.1's features, p-values and predictions on 1,243 of the release comparison's 1,430 items; the others are fits whose search met such a quotient. Predictions warn when a new row takes a feature far beyond its training range (under "Added"). The code is split into smaller modules, and the conditional re-test after the forward step without parsimony alpha is deprecated. Added ExtrapolationWarning : predict , transform and the probability methods warn when a new row takes a feature more than one width of its training range beyond that range, and say on how many rows, which features and how far; the predictions are unchanged. feature ranges holds each feature's range on the training rows. A model saved with an earlier release has no ranges and predicts as before, without the check. On tecator's own split it was raised only where a fit missed the high-fat extrapolation set by far, and on no row of the test set. Changed magnitude slots="auto" is the default , where it was 0 : 10 beam slots for regression and none for classification, whose labels carry no magnitude. The slots keep candidates whose magnitude tracks the target's, so that the search recovers laws whose parts do not correlate with the target, such as x0 x1 x2 with centred inputs. In benchmarks/release comparison/ , against 0.7.0 with the slots off, they recovered every such stress law (exact recovery 0.40 and 0.55 without them, 1.00 with), moved the held-out score of 10 of 12 real datasets by less than 0.005 (riboflavin fell by 0.011 and eyedata rose by 0.009), added a junk column to two more equations (27 of 40 against 25), and cost 1.19 times the fit time and 1.07 times the memory. Version 2.0.1 updates the article, proofs and figures and adds descriptive certificate/sign diagnostics computed from the frozen results in version 2.0.0. The complete normalized-input comparisons, Euclidean Rips entropy witnesses, synthetic tightness summaries and finite measured-EEG evaluation are retained. Readers obtain checksum-pinned O.zip from the original authors' linked repository under the source terms. Included code reconstructs the omitted arrays locally and checks their exact content and distance-matrix hashes before replaying the reported analysis. See the README and LICENSE SCOPE.md for acquisition, reproduction and reuse conditions. Original EEG source: Andrzejak et al., Physical Review E 64, 061907 (2001), 10.1103/PhysRevE.64.061907 ; dataset record: UPF e-Repositori . Evidence boundaries: analytic results are proved in the article; synthetic comparisons and the additional certificate/sign diagnostics are descriptive post-exposure analyses; the EEG evaluation uses finite references, a development-selected window and a locally frozen protocol, not public preregistration. evidence_items.summary: Abstract Accurate coding of tumor diagnoses, with the German Modification of the International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision (ICD-10-GM), and the International Classification of Diseases for Oncology, Third Edition (ICD-O-3), is essential for structured cancer documentation. Large language models (LLMs) offer opportunities for automating such tasks, but locally deployable, open-weight models often lack sufficient domain-specific coding expertise. This study investigates whether instruction-based fine-tuning on public classification resources improves the coding accuracy of open-weight LLMs for German tumor diagnosis texts. Eight models from the Qwen, Llama, and Mistral families (7–70 billion parameters) were fine-tuned on over 500,000 question-answer pairs based on the ICD-10-GM, ICD-O-3, and German procedure classification. The evaluation uses coded diagnoses from the local tumor documentation system as test data. ICD-10-GM accuracy rose from 1.4 to 24 to 41–58%, and partial (three-character codes only) accuracy from 31 to 74 to 73–83%. The accuracy of ICD-O-3 topography coding also improved but started and remained considerably lower. Malformed code outputs dropped to nearly 0% for almost all models. Tumor-diagnosis recognition reached 99%. A data quality analysis showed that incomplete diagnosis descriptions limited achievable test performance. Accuracy correlated positively with model size, but gaps between small and large models narrowed after fine-tuning. The reasoning mode in Qwen3 generally yielded lower performance than fine-tuning and was over 100 times slower. Our findings highlight the potential of leveraging public catalogues to build instruction datasets that improve LLMs in medical documentation tasks. To support reproducibility and further research, we publicly release the complete training dataset and the best-performing fine-tuned model checkpoints.
evidence_items.title: Instruction-tuning large language models with medical classification data improves ICD coding of German tumor diagnoses

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background: Clinical prediction models are trained on routine care data, and their quality in deployment depends on that data. However, data-quality assessment in healthcare AI remains largely heuristic: practitioners report missingness tables, class-balance ratios, or demographic summaries, but these numbers are not connected to what actually happens to a model trained on the data. A key open question is whether information available before training can flag which dataset conditions will harm a deployed model. Methods: We report an exploratory benchmark of a five-part, task- and target-specific data-quality profile covering: completeness (how much of the data are missing), label noise (how often recorded labels disagree with the true condition), distributional similarity (how far the training population deviates from the population the model will serve), representativeness (how well the training data cover that population), and temporal integrity (whether future information leaks into training records). Each part is an operational proxy, not a validated instrument, and carries an explicit availability state: a part that cannot be measured is reported as “not measured” rather than imputed as perfect. For every dataset condition we train a real model on the possibly corrupted data and measure how much its log-loss and calibration change on held-out patients, rather than asserting a closed-form relationship. We evaluate three cohorts from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV; Sepsis-3, N=2,000; intensive care unit (ICU) mortality, N=3,000; KDIGO-staged acute kidney injury (AKI), N=2,293) under controlled corruptions, and one external multi-institution database (eICU Collaborative Research Database, eICU-CRD; 202 hospitals). Results: Five findings emerge.
evidence_items.title: A Multidimensional Data-Quality Profile for Clinical Prediction: An Exploratory Benchmark in MIMIC-IV and eICU

evidence_items.summary: Phishing and social engineering remain the main routes to fraud against bank customers. Static warnings lose force as users habituate to them. This paper presents APUX-Bank. This paper is a synthetic benchmark for the design and evaluation of adaptive AI-based user experience (UX) models that defend bank customers against phishing. The dataset simulates a four-arm randomized experiment with 2,400 U.S. adult bank customers and 28,800 message decisions across email, SMS, voice and in-app channels. The four arms are a static warning, a rule-based adaptive warning, an AI-adaptive warning and an AI-adaptive warning with an explanation (AI-XAI). The data were generated from a seeded hierarchical logistic model. Its parameters were set from published phishing research. Logistic regression with participant-clustered errors showed that the AI-adaptive design reduced the odds of clicking a phishing message by 48 percent (OR = 0.52, 95% CI [0.45, 0.59]). The AI-XAI design reduced the odds by 56 percent (OR = 0.44, 95% CI [0.39, 0.51]). The benefit was largest for customers with low digital literacy. AI-XAI also raised usability by 6.2 points on the System Usability Scale and lowered false alarms. Trust in the system mediated 41 percent of its effect on phishing reports. The results held across GEE, random-intercept, probit and linear probability models. A parameter recovery test found that 29 of 31 true values fell inside their 95 percent confidence intervals. The data and all Python code are released for teaching, power analysis and method testing Keywords: Phishing, Social Engineering, Adaptive User Experience, Explainable Artificial Intelligence, Banking Security, Synthetic Data, Logistic Regression.
evidence_items.title: Design and evaluation of adaptive AI-based user experience models for mitigating phishing and social engineering attacks in the U.S. banking sector: A data paper with a synthetic benchmark dataset

evidence_items.summary:
OBJECTIVE
We examined how evaluation design affects comparisons of functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) short-separation correction strategies.


APPROACH
Nearest-SC, All-SC, SC-PCA and an adapted tCCA-GLM were compared in a multimodal resting-state dataset (n = 14), using semi-nested and correction-stage fully nested cross-validation, boundary purging, symmetric leave-one-modality-out (LOMO) evaluation, circular-shift nulls, injected hemodynamic response function (HRF) recovery and a second cohort.


MAIN RESULTS
In an initial joint-target diagnostic analysis, the adapted tCCA-GLM's absolute out-of-fold R² increased by 42.7 percentage points from semi-nested to purged fully nested evaluation. In a separate fixed-seed purged analysis, its null-adjusted ΔR² was -1.1%. Symmetric LOMO, which evaluates reduced tCCA models, yielded no statistically detected method differences (all paired p ≥ 0.3685), but did not establish equivalence or separately quantify leakage and input-target overlap. Motion-targeted external validation provided partial support for an evaluation-tier × method interaction (Freedman-Lane p < 0.005). SC-PCA had lower mean known-truth normalized root mean square error (nRMSE = 0.037) than the adapted tCCA-GLM (0.121); within-metric Holm-adjusted comparisons were significant for this contrast and for amplitude-bias comparisons with all three SC-based strategies, but not for slopes. Sensitivity analyses included training-fold PCA selection, LOMO boundary/segment-filtering checks, lagged evaluation and longer test blocks.


SIGNIFICANCE
Benchmarks should fit learned correction stages within training data, disclose correction-evaluation overlap and assess signal preservation separately. Findings are specific to the evaluated implementations, outcomes and datasets; the sensitivity analyses do not establish complete removal of preprocessing-related dependence.
evidence_items.title: Correction-stage information leakage and target-input asymmetry can distort comparisons of fNIRS short-separation channel correction strategies.

evidence_items.summary: Modern expressive Text-to-Speech (TTS) systems for adult speech can generate highly expressive speech when provided with a sufficient amount of training data. However, expressive TTS systems for children are often restricted and have been under-explored to date. Child TTS systems’ challenges arise from the scarcity of training datasets, difficulties in accessing them publicly, and various issues associated with these datasets, including noisy data and indiscernible speech. This work introduces an expressive Multi-Style Child TTS in low-resource settings. Our model stands as the first expressive TTS model designed specifically for children. It is a style-based generative model based on the StyleTTS architecture. Our model is trained on an expressive ChildTinyTalks (CTT) dataset, comprising 2 h of speech, covering four speaking styles. We verify the framework through subjective and objective evaluations and demonstrate that Multi-Style Child TTS outperforms other baseline models.
evidence_items.title: Multi-Style Child TTS: An Expressive Text-to-Speech System for Children in Low-Resource Scenarios

evidence_items.summary: AI agents that operate external tools can continue acting after a user narrows their permissions, creating a security problem that final-state evaluation may fail to detect. Existing agent benchmarks commonly emphasize task completion or resulting state, but those outcomes do not reveal whether an unauthorized operation was proposed, approved, dispatched, or merely prevented by a downstream error. We investigate permission withdrawal as a trajectory-level authorization problem and evaluate whether runtime gates can preserve revised permissions while allowing agents to complete work that remains authorized. Two acting models were tested in a deterministic tool environment under prompt-only execution, a rule-based reference gate, and a model-based gate. A 72-episode diagnostic examined two previously exposed write workflows, followed by a separately frozen 384-episode extension spanning eight new tasks and four authorization mechanisms. In the diagnostic, prompt-only agents executed forbidden same-value writes in two episodes; both runtime gates prevented forbidden execution, although the model gate falsely rejected three authorized calls. In the extension, 346 of 384 episodes completed safely and 383 preserved the required protected state. No forbidden request executed successfully, yet the model gate approved three unauthorized requests that were stopped only because the referenced resources did not exist. The results demonstrate that correct final state and zero forbidden execution can still conceal failures in authorization reasoning. We contribute a replayable evaluation framework that separates proposals, gate decisions, dispatch, state transitions, and useful completion, enabling more precise assessment of security controls for tool-using agents.
evidence_items.title: Permission Withdrawal in Tool-Using Language Model Agents: Runtime Enforcement and Recovery

evidence_items.summary:
INTRODUCTION
Current AI models for optical coherence tomography (OCT) primarily focus on diagnosis as a standalone task. We developed and validated an end-to-end agentic AI workflow that integrates automated macular hole (MH) diagnosis from OCT images with structured patient-friendly report generation.


METHODS
The proposed sequential workflow coordinated by a workflow orchestration agent consisted of an image diagnosis stage and a language generation step. The OCT version of RETFound, a self-supervised retinal foundation model, was fine-tuned for binary classification of macular OCT scans as MH or normal macula. Training, validation, and internal testing were performed using multiple public OCT datasets with patient-level stratified splitting, followed by external validation on two independent datasets. The performance of the fine-tuned foundation model was evaluated using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC AUC). For each new OCT image, the AI agent used the trained RETFound model to classify the image, received the diagnostic output, incorporated it into a structured prompt, and called the large language model (GPT-4) to generate the clinical report.


RESULTS
On the internal test set (n = 180), the model achieved an accuracy of 100% (95% confidence interval (CI), 97.9-100%) with an AUC of 1.00. On external validation (n = 1014), accuracy was 98.8% (95% CI 97.9-99.3%), sensitivity was 97.9% (95% CI 96.3-98.8%), specificity was 100% (95% CI 99.2-100.0%), and AUC was 0.999 (95% CI 0.998-1.000). Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) analysis showed that predictions were driven by relevant retinal regions, particularly the macular hole and adjacent layers. The end-to-end agentic AI workflow generated concise and standardized patient-friendly reports for all samples, without the language model influencing diagnostic decisions.


CONCLUSIONS
This study demonstrates the feasibility of an end-to-end AI workflow coordinated by a workflow orchestration agent for robust OCT-based MH diagnosis with a large language model for structured report generation. By separating image-based diagnosis from language generation, this approach offers a practical and scalable solution for virtual vitreoretinal clinics.
evidence_items.title: An Agentic AI Workflow for Automated Macular Hole Diagnosis and Structured Report Generation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that plan, remember, call tools, coordinate with other agents and act over long horizons with limited supervision. Evidence on whether such agents work reliably is scattered and sometimes contradictory, and recent reviews largely describe architectures, benchmarks or threats in isolation. This systematic, taxonomy-driven critical review follows PRISMA 2020 reporting where applicable, without meta-analytic pooling, and synthesises 98 verified sources published up to 30 June 2026. It differs from prior reviews in four ways. First, it weighs evidence: eight headline claims are graded by an explicit rule, and contradictions are traced to moderators such as feedback source, equal-compute comparison and task verifiability. Second, it specifies a closed-loop reference framework operationally, adding a verification stage and a safety-and-authorisation gate, and codes ten published systems against it; none fully implements both control stages. Third, it links capabilities to evaluation hooks, readiness levels and re-assurance triggers for agents that change after deployment. Fourth, its evidence base is auditable through re-executed searches with measured recall, verified references and a released evidence matrix. High-confidence findings are that intrinsic self-correction is unreliable, long-horizon autonomous planning remains weak and tool-using agents are broadly vulnerable to injection. Multi-agent benefits are conditional (moderate confidence), whereas claims about benchmark validity and memory consistency rest mainly on preprints. A reliability model quantifies the value of independent verification, and an eighteen-direction roadmap is ranked by an explicit priority rule.
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI for Complex Decision-Making: A Systematic Critical Review of Planning, Memory, Tools, Safety and Assurance in Autonomous Systems

evidence_items.summary: Software defect prediction (SDP) is an important task in software engineering that aims to identify defect-prone software components before deployment, thereby supporting software reliability and reducing maintenance effort. Recent advances in pre-trained transformer models (PTMs) have demonstrated considerable potential for source-code understanding and automated defect detection. However, comparisons of transformer-based models across previous studies are often complicated by differences in datasets, preprocessing procedures, training configurations, and evaluation protocols. This study presents a focused literature overview and a controlled empirical benchmarking evaluation of four widely used transformer-based models BERT Base, DistilBERT, RoBERTa, and CodeBERT—for software defect prediction using the CodeXGLUE-Devign dataset. Rather than proposing a new model architecture, the study investigates the comparative behavior of existing pre-trained transformer models under a common experimental configuration. To reduce dependence on a single random initialization, each model is independently fine-tuned and evaluated using five random seeds, resulting in 20 training runs. Performance is assessed using Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-score, with results reported as mean ± standard deviation across the five runs. Pairwise differences are further examined using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test with Holm correction for multiple comparisons. The experimental results show that CodeBERT achieves the highest mean Accuracy (72.69 ± 0.88%), Precision (74.33 ± 1.75%), and F1-score (66.60 ± 1.67%), whereas BERT Base obtains the highest mean Recall (61.48 ± 3.07%). DistilBERT achieves an Accuracy of 69.29 ± 0.87% and an F1-score of 64.33 ± 1.48% while requiring substantially less training time than the larger models. RoBERTa exhibits lower and considerably more variable performance across the five runs. Nevertheless, none of the pairwise performance differences remain statistically significant at α = 0.05 after Holm correction. The findings demonstrate the importance of repeated-run evaluation, statistical analysis, class-wise assessment, error analysis, and computational considerations when benchmarking transformer-based models for SDP. The study therefore provides replication-oriented empirical evidence concerning the performance, stability, error characteristics, and computational trade-offs of existing transformer architectures under a controlled experimental setting.
evidence_items.title: A structured overview and empirical evaluation of fine-tuning pre-trained transformer models for software defect prediction

evidence_items.summary: Diagnostic imaging represents one of the most promising clinical applications of artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the customised convolutional neural network (CNN) SepNetDense for distinguishing between normal and abnormal canine brain magnetic resonance images (MRIs), with the aim of enhancing diagnostic efficiency and assisting radiologists in identifying abnormal images. The dataset comprised T1-weighted (T1w) pre- and post-contrast sequences in transverse, sagittal, and dorsal planes from 550 dogs, collected from four universities. Dogs were included if they had a complete clinical diagnosis confirmed either through histopathology or in accordance with current clinical consensus. Patients were randomly divided into a training set (n = 444), a validation set (n = 53), and a test set (n = 53). Each MRI was labelled on a slice-by-slice basis as normal or abnormal. The model was trained on 205 normal imaging datasets (e.g., extracranial aetiologies, idiopathic epilepsy, paroxysmal dyskinesia) and 239 abnormal ones (e.g., neoplasms, inflammatory lesions, other pathologies). The model correctly predicted 74% of the true normal slices in the test set as normal and 73% of the true abnormal as abnormal. A ROC analysis of the model’s prediction at the patient level revealed that, at a threshold of 51% abnormal slices per patient, the model reached an optimal balance of 83% sensitivity (95% CI 67–91%) and 78% (95% CI 54–91%) specificity, with a balanced accuracy of 80% (95% CI 69–92%). ANCOVA revealed that the CNN’s classification performance was influenced by multiple biological, technical, and institutional factors. Lesion diagnosis, institutional setting, and breed size had significant large effects, whereas body weight showed a significant medium effect. Significant interactions with large effect sizes were also observed between diagnosis and institute, as well as between breed size and weight. Additionally, a distinct pattern was observed in the distribution of prediction categories along the anatomical axes, with a trend towards better CNN performance in the central quartiles across all MRI sequences. Overall, the results demonstrate the feasibility of CNN-assisted triage of canine brain MRI studies and highlight diagnosis, institutional setting, breed size, and body weight as key determinants of model performance, emphasising the importance of heterogeneous datasets for the development of robust veterinary AI applications.
evidence_items.title: CNN model-based image classification for canine brain MRI abnormalities

authors: Puteri Fatin Nurul Izzati Mohamed Fadil
evidence_items.summary: Class imbalance remains a major challenge in multiclass Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS), particularly when rare attack categories are insufficiently represented during model training. Although oversampling techniques are widely used to address this issue, their effectiveness may vary depending on the sampling strategy, classifier, and distribution of attack categories. This study compares Adaptive Synthetic Sampling (ADASYN) and Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique combined with Edited Nearest Neighbors (SMOTE-ENN) to investigate their effects on multiclass intrusion detection using the UNSW-NB15 dataset. ADASYN was selected for its adaptive generation of synthetic samples in difficult-to-learn minority-class regions, whereas SMOTE-ENN combines minority-class oversampling with neighborhood based data cleaning to reduce potentially noisy or overlapping instances. Their effectiveness was evaluated against an unbalanced baseline using Random Forest (RF), Decision Tree (DT), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and a hybrid Convolutional Neural Network–Long Short-Term Memory (CNN-LSTM) model. The experiments assessed accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score using the held-out test set. The results indicate that the impact of resampling is classifier-dependent. CNN-LSTM combined with SMOTE-ENN achieved the highest reported overall performance, with 90% accuracy, 87% precision, 83% recall, and 84% F1-score. These findings demonstrate the potential benefits of combining hybrid resampling with deep learning for multiclass NIDS, while highlighting the importance of evaluating sampling strategies across different classification models and attack categories.
evidence_items.title: A Comparative Study of ADASYN and SMOTE-ENN for Class Imbalance in Intrusion Detection Systems

evidence_items.summary: The digitization of multilingual library collections requires text recognition that copes with diverse scripts, writing styles and document structures. Optical Character Recognition (OCR) remains central to this process, but recognition of cursive scripts such as Arabic and Urdu is still difficult. This paper presents a multilingual OCR integration framework for digital library applications that combines classical image preprocessing (Otsu binarization, Hough-based skew correction and morphological filtering; no learned preprocessing), two pre-trained deep learning OCR engines (PaddleOCR and MMOCR) used in inference mode, a fully specified token-level fusion procedure, and a language-sensitive post-processing module. The contribution is at the system-engineering level: the structured integration of existing components into a reproducible multilingual pipeline, with formally defined evaluation protocols and a link to OCR-enabled language coverage analytics. The framework is evaluated on two public benchmarks, the ICDAR 2019 MLT19 scene-text dataset (English, Hindi, Chinese, Arabic) and the synthetic printed Urdu dataset MMU-OCR-21, covering five languages in four script families. Post-processing reduced the average Character Error Rate (CER) from 0.188 to 0.107 (mean per-language relative reduction 42.6%) and the average Word Error Rate (WER) from 0.272 to 0.156, with statistically significant gains for all five languages (paired t-test, p < 0.001). In the fusion ablation, dual-engine fusion alone did not reduce average CER relative to the stronger single engine, so the measured gains are attributed mainly to preprocessing and post-processing. A Language Coverage Index (LCI) is introduced to quantify the share of languages whose OCR output meets a working CER threshold (θacc = 0.15); the LCI rose from 40% to 100% on the benchmark test partition. A supplementary evaluation on 150 digitized library pages from the Internet Archive showed a smaller but consistent CER reduction (37.3%) and an LCI of 60%, with Arabic and Urdu remaining above the threshold, and identified historical typefaces and multi-column layouts as priority challenges. Because the primary evaluation uses scene-text and synthetic word images, the results indicate directional promise rather than deployment readiness; full-scale validation on institutional library collections is the main direction for future work.
evidence_items.title: AI‑based multilingual OCR and OCR-enabled collection diversity analytics in libraries

evidence_items.summary: Cross-institutional labor-risk assessment involves sensitive records, class imbalance, and substantial distributional heterogeneity. This study presents DP-PFLR, a personalized federated-learning framework integrating Adaptive Privacy Budget Allocation (APBA), Risk-Aware Re-weighting (RAR), and Personalized Heterogeneity-aware Aggregation (PHA). APBA combines private adaptive clipping with an RDP-calibrated noise schedule; RAR combines focal loss with inverse-prevalence client weighting; and PHA retains personalized heads locally while aggregating the shared encoder. The framework provides record-level differential privacy for the server-visible training transcript, whereas local heads are not themselves differentially private. Experiments on Adult, IBM-HR, and OSHA evaluate income status, employee attrition, and establishment-level occupational risk under proxy cross-silo partitions. At the target budget \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$(\varepsilon ,\delta )=(4,10^{-5})$$\end{document}, the maximum accounted privacy loss was 3.99. DP-PFLR achieved macro-F1 scores of 0.792, 0.695, and 0.650, respectively, exceeding the strongest evaluated private baseline on all three datasets. Paired tests, complete \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$2^3$$\end{document} ablation, sensitivity analysis, and restrictive-privacy and robustness experiments further supported the framework’s privacy–utility performance. evidence_items.summary: Cell segmentation is a critical yet under-standardized step in spatial transcriptomics, directly affecting cell identity assignment, spatial organization and downstream biological interpretation. Despite rapid advances in spatial transcriptomics technologies, systematic evaluations of segmentation methods across platforms and biological contexts remain limited. Here we benchmark 11 image-based, transcriptomics-based and multimodal segmentation methods across 15 datasets generated by 5 spatial transcriptomics technologies, spanning 12 human and mouse tissue types. We introduce biologically informed evaluation metrics that quantify segmentation quality, transcript recovery, cell composition, morphology, expression purity and spatial organization. Benchmarking reveals substantial variation in performance across datasets, technologies and evaluation criteria, highlighting trade-offs among segmentation completeness, transcriptomic fidelity and biological interpretability. Cross-technology analyses further demonstrate that segmentation choice critically shapes downstream analyses, including cell-type specificity, transcript contamination and ligand-receptor inference. Together, our unified Nextflow pipeline provides a scalable foundation for standardized evaluation of segmentation and method selection in spatial transcriptomics.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking segmentation methods for spatial transcriptomics.

evidence_items.summary: To improve the detection performance of anomalous network traffic, a network anomaly traffic detection model was developed by integrating an improved Remora Optimization Algorithm (IROA) with Support Vector Machine (SVM). Specifically, the White Shark Optimizer was incorporated into the host-switching mechanism of the Remora Optimization Algorithm to enhance global exploration. An adaptive weight operator was adopted to refine the experiential attack process, thus improving the convergence accuracy. In addition, a quadratic interpolation strategy was embedded to strengthen the global search performance and the ability to escape local optima. The performance of IROA is first evaluated on the CEC2020 (dim = 10) and CEC2017 (dim = 50, 100) benchmark functions, confirming its superior convergence speed and robustness in high-dimensional search spaces. Subsequently, the IROA-SVM model is validated on the NSL-KDD dataset, with comprehensive comparisons against seven optimization-based SVM models and three conventional classifiers. Statistical significance is rigorously verified using the Friedman rank test (p = 0.0008) and pairwise Wilcoxon rank-sum tests (all \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textrm{p} < 0.05$$\end{document}). Results demonstrate that IROA-SVM achieves the highest performance across Accuracy, Precision, F1-score, ROC-AUC, and MCC. However, the inherently high computational complexity of IROA and the outdated nature of the NSL-KDD dataset limit its direct applicability to real-time detection in modern network environments. These limitations and corresponding future research directions are explicitly discussed.
evidence_items.title: An improved remora optimization algorithm for optimizing a support vector machine based network anomaly traffic detection model

evidence_items.summary: This dataset accompanies the research study entitled “Causality-Aware Risk-Sensitive Economic Action Selection for Battery-Constrained Deep Reinforcement Learning in Renewable Microgrid Energy Management.” The dataset provides processed, hourly renewable microgrid data for developing and evaluating a causality-aware, risk-sensitive economic action-selection method (RSE-AS) applied to battery energy storage management with Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) reinforcement learning. Dataset contents Training (2017–2020): 35,064 hourly observations. Validation (2021): 8,760 hourly observations. Testing (2022): 8,760 hourly observations. Additional testing (2023): 8,753 hourly observations, ending December 31, 2023, at 16:00 UTC. Out-of-distribution evaluation (2022): Four controlled scenarios comprising a 20% increase in demand, a 30% reduction in photovoltaic generation, a 50% increase in electricity tariffs, and a combined perturbation scenario. The processed files include electricity demand, photovoltaic generation, electricity tariffs, forecast information, uncertainty estimates, and temporal features. To support causal decision-making, the evaluation workflow constructs decision-time observations using lagged load, photovoltaic generation, one-hour-ahead net-load forecasts, and uncertainty estimates. Temporal alignment and forecast-target timestamps were checked during dataset validation. Original data sources Electricity demand: Hourly Electricity Demand Profiles for Each County in the Contiguous United States . DOI: https://doi.org/10.25984/3366592 Solar resource: National Solar Radiation Database (NSRDB) . DOI: https://doi.org/10.25984/1810289 The processed data are derived from these sources and include research-specific transformations. Both original sources are attributed in the accompanying DATA SOURCES.md file. Data availability and reuse The archive contains eight processed CSV files, a README, data-source attribution, and licensing information.
evidence_items.title: RSE-AS: Processed Causal Microgrid Dataset and Out-of-Distribution Scenarios (2017–2023)

evidence_items.summary: Abstract: The rapid growth of social media and online platforms has generated large volumes of opinion-rich text, increasing the need for automated sentiment analysis. Traditional machine learning methods can efficiently classify text but often have limited ability to capture semantic context, negation, sarcasm, and domain-specific expressions, whereas modern contextual models such as BERT provide richer representations at higher computational cost. This paper surveys research on context-aware sentiment analysis published from 2020 to 2026 and categorizes existing approaches according to their representation and classification techniques. Based on the identified trends and limitations, a hybrid opinion-mining framework is proposed that combines text preprocessing, TF-IDF statistical features, TextBlob lexical polarity, BERT contextual representations, and CNN-BiLSTM with attention mechanisms for sentiment classification and emotion recognition. The surveyed studies, datasets, reported findings, advantages, and limitations are comparatively discussed to identify research gaps. The analysis highlights the potential of combining complementary statistical, lexical, contextual, and sequential representations while also emphasizing challenges related to computational complexity, sarcasm, negation, multilingualism, and domain adaptation. The proposed framework provides a structured basis for future empirical evaluation across multiple domains.
evidence_items.title: A Context-Aware Hybrid Model for Sentiment Analysis

evidence_items.summary: Neural vocoders are central to speech synthesis; despite their success, most still suffer from limited pitch (F0) modeling and inaccurate phase reconstruction. We propose a vocoder that introduces F0-guided harmonic attention to enhance voiced-segment encoding and directly predicts complex-spectral components for waveform synthesis via inverse STFT. Unlike mel-spectrogram–based approaches, our design jointly models magnitude and phase, ensuring phase coherence and improved pitch fidelity. To further align with perceptual quality, we adopt a multi-objective training strategy that integrates adversarial, spectral, and phase-aware losses. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate consistent gains over HiFi-GAN and AutoVocoder: F0-RMSE reduced by 22%, voiced/unvoiced error lowered by 18%, and MOS scores improved by 0.15. These results show that F0-guided attention combined with direct complex-spectrum modeling yields more natural, pitch-accurate, and robust synthetic speech, setting a strong foundation for expressive neural vocoding.
evidence_items.title: Prosody-Guided Harmonic Attention for Phase-Coherent Neural Vocoding in the Complex Spectrum

evidence_items.summary: Emotional intelligence in synthetic speech remains a critical challenge in human-machine interaction, despite significant advances in the naturalness and intelligibility of speech synthesis. Current systems struggle to accurately capture the nuanced emotional expressions characteristic of human speech, including rapid pitch transitions, wide frequency variations, and irregular vibrato patterns. While pitch estimation algorithms like PESTO and FCPE have proven effective for standard speech, their performance on emotionally expressive content remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we present ESCAPE, a novel algorithm specifically designed for emotional speech processing. ESCAPE combines PESTO's precision in handling frequency variations with FCPE's context- aware processing through a hybrid architecture, enabling robust pitch tracking in expressive vocal content. Our approach excels at capturing complex acoustic patterns unique to emotional utterances while maintaining computational efficiency. We provide the first comprehensive evaluation of PESTO and FCPE on emotional speech datasets and demonstrate ESCAPE's transformative potential for pitch estimation in emotionally expressive speech synthesis. The results showcase significant progress in bridging the gap between human-like emotional expression and machine- generated speech, marking a pivotal advancement in emotional speech synthesis technology.
evidence_items.title: A Hybrid Algorithm for Robust Pitch Estimation in Emotional Speech Synthesis

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can convert long documents into structured research variables. Auditability becomes difficult when evidence selection and model scoring are not stored. We study an inspectable scoring workflow that converts archived annual-report Evidence Packs into a five-dimension digital-transformation disclosure score. The design combines report selection, PDF-to-text normalization, bounded paragraph retrieval, and DeepSeek rubric scoring through a strict JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) interface; the original canonical prompt/run binding is not available. We evaluate three measurement questions and one secondary utility check: reproducible Evidence Pack construction, LLM–human agreement on shared Evidence Packs, ordinal error/confusion diagnostics, and non-causal panel-use stress tests. The evaluation panel contains 476 firm-year observations from 64 firms for 2013–2024. The post-validation score shows high internal coherence for the additive rubric (Cronbach’s α = 0.893; first principal component explains 0.704 of standardized dimensional variance), substantial within-firm variation (mean within-firm standard deviation (SD) 2.901; 92.19% non-zero), and strong LLM–human agreement on shared Evidence Packs (total-score Spearman 0.910, Pearson 0.921, mean absolute error (MAE) 1.273; dimension-level weighted kappa 0.665–0.823). Human–Human total-score reliability, measured by the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), is ICC(2,1) = 0.811. Baseline comparisons show lower error than frozen lexicon-count and firm-grouped term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) Ridge alternatives (MAE = 1.273 vs . 6.387 and 2.737). A 96-record rule-based retrieval audit shows high mean dimension coverage (0.936) but incomplete heuristic paragraph recall@30 (micro recall = 0.419); four audited zero-hit packs are false empty (4.17%). The main reliability claim is therefore bounded to shared archived evidence.
evidence_items.title: Auditable large language model scoring of annual-report evidence packs: human calibration, baselines, and reproducibility checks

evidence_items.summary: Objective To conduct a systematic bibliometric review of artificial intelligence (AI)-based multimodal neuroimaging research in depression, mapping its evolution, collaborative networks, and intellectual foundations to guide future translation.Methods Records were retrieved from Web of Science Core Collection (search date: 1 September 2025) using terms for depression, neuroimaging modalities, and AI/machine learning (ML)/deep learning. English, peer-reviewed articles/reviews (2001–2025) were screened; 1,232 studies were retained after deduplication and filtering. Analyses included annual output trends, co-authorship networks (countries/institutions/authors), keyword co-occurrence clustering with burst detection, and co-citation/bibliographic coupling using VOSviewer (v1.6.20) and Bibliometrix (v4.5.1).Results Annual publications rose from <20/year to 202 in 2024; 2025 counts (n=173) reflect January–August only. The international network spans 42 countries/regions linked by 320 co-authorship ties (total link strength=1,228; density of approximately 0.37). USA, China, and the UK constitute the epistemic core, with expanding participation from India, Brazil, and Iran. Institutional and author overlays indicate a small-world, hierarchical organization (205 institutions; 10 collaboration communities; author network 168 researchers) characterized by a productive core and long tail. Six keyword clusters delineate a functional workflow: 1) biomarkers/phenotypes, 2) functional connectivity, 3) machine-learning/computational approaches, 4) multimodal/precision psychiatry, 5) diagnostic classification/algorithm development, and 6) structural imaging/comorbidity. Co-citation and coupling reveal a progression from early ML and connectivity foundations to deep/graph models, multimodal fusion, explainability, and treatment-oriented prediction.Conclusion AI-based multimodal neuroimaging in depression has evolved into a coherent, translationally focused field.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Multimodal Neuroimaging Research on Depression: A Bibliometric Analysis

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Automated regression testing is essential for maintaining rapid, high-quality delivery in Agile and Scrum organizations. Many teams, including Hacon (a Siemens company), face a persistent gap: validated test specifications accumulate faster than they are automated, limiting regression coverage and increasing manual work. This paper reports an exploratory industrial case study of the Hacon Test Automation Copilot, an agentic AI system that generates system-level regression test scripts from validated specifications using retrieval-augmented generation and a multi-agent workflow. Integrated with Hacon’s CI pipelines, the Copilot operates asynchronously as a “silent AI teammate”, producing candidate scripts for human review. Mixed-method evaluation shows the AI accelerates script authoring and increases throughput, with 30–50% code reuse. However, human review remains necessary for maintainability and correct domain interpretation. Clear specifications, explicit governance, and ongoing human–AI collaboration are critical. We conclude with lessons for scaling regression automation and enabling effective human–AI teaming in Agile settings.
evidence_items.title: Human–AI Collaboration for Scaling Agile Regression Testing: An Agentic-AI Teammate from Manual to Automated Testing
