evidence_items.summary: Automated accessibility checkers can identify WCAG violations but cannot resolve them, leaving remediation as a manual burden for developers. Large language models (LLMs) have been proposed as a means of generating code-level fixes, yet their effectiveness on unmodified production code remains largely untested. This poster evaluates GPT-5.5 and LLaMA-3.3 on remediating WCAG 2.2 violations naturally occurring across ten real-world websites spanning seven domains, using four prompting strategies: Zero-Shot, Few-Shot, In-Context Learning, and Chain-of-Thought. This poster showcases that LLaMA outperforms GPT overall (45.58% vs. 37.6%), with CoT yielding the highest accuracy for LLaMA and Few-Shot for GPT. While a combined-model approach raises the fix rate to 49.26%, both models fail on semantically demanding violations like missing image alt text, revealing a fundamental grounding limitation. We translate these findings into concrete recommendations for practitioners building LLM-assisted accessibility tools and for researchers designing future evaluations.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Web Accessibility Remediation in Real-World Websites

evidence_items.summary: Digital accessibility barriers are easier to prevent during design than to remediate after implementation, yet accessibility is often taught and practiced as a downstream concern. Despite growing attention in computing and design education, accessibility efforts continue to emphasize code-level auditing, remediation, and compliance checking, with less attention to early design decisions. The shift-left principle seeks to address this gap by embedding accessibility from the initial UX design phase, but its adoption remains limited. To explore how AI can support this shift, we developed a Figma plugin that uses a multimodal large language model (LLM) to evaluate UI frames against WCAG criteria and provide contextual, design-stage feedback. In a three-week deployment, 89 practicing professionals and computing or design students used the plugin alongside existing tools (Stark and Axe for Designers) and reported their perceptions, experiences, and self-reported abilities through pre- and post-use surveys. Overall, 92.1% reported identifying accessibility issues earlier, 96.6% reported productivity gains, and participants rated recommendation likelihood (M=4.25/5) and generated specification accuracy (M=4.08/5) highly. Findings also suggest that contextual AI feedback can help learners identify and reason about accessibility issues earlier in the design process. We conclude with practical takeaways for integrating AI-supported tools into accessibility education.
evidence_items.title: Designing and Evaluating an AI-Powered Figma Plugin for Accessibility Education

evidence_items.summary: As large language model (LLM)-based voice agents increasingly enter high-risk domains such as medical recommendation, voice personality is becoming a key social cue for trust. Yet research has largely focused on sighted users, leaving how blind users interpret these cues unclear. To address this gap, we conducted a two-part exploratory study with blind participants. We first created four theory-inspired voice probes varying intended warmth and competence, and ran a participatory co-design workshop (N=6) supported by tactile toolkits. This approach enabled participants to directly experience, evaluate, and articulate their perceptions. Our findings show how the two features (acoustic and linguistic) relate to perceived warmth and competence, which jointly shape trust judgments. To further examine these insights in a more realistic interaction context, we conducted a follow-up within-subject study (N = 11). Across both studies, blind users consistently prioritized competence over warmth in medical decision-making. Together, these findings contribute design knowledge and methods for building trustworthy and accessible voice agents in risk-sensitive contexts.
evidence_items.title: Exploring How Warmth and Competence Shape Trust in Medical Voice Agents with Blind Users

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in settings that affect disabled people, but little is known about how these systems represent disability stereotypes in the Chinese social context. We compare the three-dimensional stereotype profiles of six disability groups in China across a non-disabled public sample (N = 176), a self-identified disability community sample (N = 51), and four LLMs (ChatGPT 5.4, Claude 4.6 Sonnet, Qwen3-Max, and DeepSeek-Chat V3.2; 50 independent application programming interface (API) calls for each model, temperature, and disability group; 2,400 valid responses). The main human materials and LLM prompts were in Mandarin Chinese. A later English-prompt robustness set used the same models, temperatures, and disability groups and produced a similar profile. Three results are central. First, humans and models preserve the same broad hierarchy: physical and sensory disabilities are rated more positively than intellectual and psychiatric disability (human-human profile r = .987; human-LLM r = .82 to .94 when temperatures are pooled). Second, the models rate courage above the human baseline (model-level difference +0.38 to +0.76) and show much less within-condition variability than either human sample (mean cell standard deviation (SD) 0.02-0.09 vs. 0.90 and 0.94). Third, the closest human reference varies by model: the two U.S.-built models are closer to the non-disabled public sample, whereas the two China-built models are slightly closer to the disability community sample. Because we evaluated only four commercial models, we treat this model-origin pattern as descriptive, not causal. In this setting, LLMs preserve the structure of disability stigma while raising courage ratings and narrowing observed response variability.
evidence_items.title: Preserved Hierarchy, Inflated Courage: How Four LLMs Re-inscribe Chinese Disability Stereotypes Across Public and Community Perspectives

evidence_items.summary: Sidewalk images are increasingly used to support route planning for people facing mobility challenges, but interpreting them one by one remains a burden. While recent work has explored automatic extraction of accessibility information from such images, two gaps remain: whether large language models (LLMs) can accurately describe sidewalk problems, and whether these descriptions reflect the perspectives across mobility groups. To address these gaps, we evaluated LLM-generated sidewalk image descriptions from the perspectives of perceived accuracy and user-centered relevance. We compared four conditions combining generation format (monologue or dialogue) and role setting (generic or participant-matched role), based on evaluations by 12 participants, including manual wheelchair users, cane users, and stroller users. The results showed that, in the evaluated pipeline, dialogue-based generation did not clearly improve perceived accuracy, whereas participant-matched role assignment improved user-centered relevance. We also found that, without explicit role assignment, the evaluated LLM tended to adopt a wheelchair-user perspective as the implicit default, with additional checks suggesting a similar but model-dependent bias in other LLMs. Based on these findings, we derive design implications for sidewalk image description systems that better accommodate needs across mobility groups.
evidence_items.title: Can Dialogue and Role Improve LLM Sidewalk Image Descriptions Across Mobility Groups?

evidence_items.summary: Fully autonomous ride-hailing services (FARS) promise new independence for blind and low-vision (BLV) travelers, yet research remains largely anticipatory. Surveys, proxies, and staged enactments dominate, leaving the lived experience of deployed, commercial FARS nearly unexamined. We conducted a qualitative interview study with five BLV riders who frequently use human-operated ride-hailing and have completed multiple Waymo trips, benchmarking FARS against human-driven rides. Data comprised semi-structured Zoom interviews of 75 minutes, transcribed and analyzed via reflexive thematic analysis. Four themes emerged. Riders described recovered autonomy and ownership, comparative trust with a privacy inversion favoring corporate over human-driver recording, pickup and drop-off as critical failure points around an otherwise friction-free ride, and design pathways toward an assisted FARS model. We reframe driverless ride-hailing as restructuring rather than removing the assistance relationship, relocating support from driver to system. These findings motivate multimodal, embodied assistance for accessibility researchers, designers, and developers.
evidence_items.title: It’s Our Ride, We’re Just Out of the Driver’s Seat: Perceptions of and Challenges with Fully Autonomous Vehicles Among BLV Waymo Riders

evidence_items.summary: Absorption and scattering coefficients for the Jerlov optical water types, taken from the primary literature with the provenance of every value recorded. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Twenty-five entries are documented, nine of them confirmed defects in the source literature: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7, a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients, a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset, and a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten. Three further entries were open questions that obtaining the 1968 first edition settled. The same Jerlov water type is in circulation with beam attenuations differing by a factor of five, which is why every coefficient here carries the source it came from. Every shipped table can be regenerated from its primary source by the scripts in tools/ , and each generation step checks the result against the equations of the paper it came from.
evidence_items.title: jerlov: inherent optical properties of the Jerlov optical water types, with provenance

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains the derived, privacy-screened data underlying the article "Coordinated Amplification and Organic Virality: State Narratives and Netizen Voices in the Digital Discourse of Kalimantan's 2026 Forest and Land Fires." It comprises 997 social media posts collected via social listening from six platforms (Twitter/X, Threads, TikTok, Facebook, Instagram, and YouTube) using the keywords "karhutla" and "Kalimantan" during 1-10 August 2026, classified into three diffusion-mechanism categories (Coordinated Amplification, Organic Virality, Unique/Individual Content) and three actor types (Government/Institution, Media, Citizen/Non-institutional). Account names and source URLs are included only for government/institutional and media accounts; these fields are redacted for posts from private, non-institutional citizen accounts to protect individual privacy, consistent with the ethical considerations described in the associated article. Full post text is not included, as the authors do not hold redistribution rights to the verbatim content of third-party social media posts. See the README sheet within this file for full documentation of the classification methodology and a complete list of exclusions and their rationale.
evidence_items.title: Underlying Data: Coordinated Amplification and Organic Virality in the Digital Discourse of Kalimantan's 2026 Forest and Land Fires

evidence_items.summary: Research software, source data and reproducibility evidence accompanying “What weighted sums miss: linear cell bounds and quantitative continuity of sparse interval certificates”. The package contains exact certificate producers and checkers, continuous sparse conversion, a regularity diagnostic and retained computational studies. Supplementary Software 1 supplies the compact core and the current runtime, with the source versions needed for the reported results identified separately. Supplementary Software 2 preserves the speculative-discovery study, including its adverse continuation decision. Supplementary Software 3 supplies exact regularity diagnostics and a classifier catalogue using the UCI Default of Credit Card Clients dataset. The original ID split and the single post-hoc sensitivity are retained separately. Grouping all 23 raw fields prevents identical raw-feature groups crossing those sensitivity partitions; overlap after projection to the 19 fitting predictors remains. The resulting certificates use one cell and support two. Their exactness concerns the empirical loss tables, not population generalisation. Source Data.zip supplies numerical and analytic figure inputs. Figures editable.zip supplies editable ODG sources and figure exports. Current Reproducibility Data.zip supplies the selected benchmark observations, proof objects, protocols and source dependencies supporting comparisons in the current article and Supplementary Information. The complete private development history and journal manuscript documents are excluded. DEPOSIT README.txt identifies the components; SHA256SUMS.txt records their identities. Distribution version 1.0.0 preserves runtime baseline 0.1.0-dev.10. Reported scientific results retain their original scope and generating source identities. evidence_items.summary: Automatic facial emotion recognition is a key tool in applications such as human-computer interaction, emotional monitoring, and AI-assisted educational environments. This study evaluates the performance of three deep learning architectures in classifying facial expressions corresponding to seven basic emotions. A curated dataset of 20,000 images was built by merging and refining multiple public sources. The images were preprocessed using face detection, resizing to 224×224 pixels, and data augmentation techniques to improve generalization. Three models were implemented: a baseline convolutional neural network (CNN) developed from scratch, a pretrained DenseNet121 architecture with fine-tuning, and an optimized version of ResNet50 incorporating LeakyReLU activation, L2 regularization, label smoothing, and progressive fine-tuning. The results show that while the baseline CNN exhibits limitations in accuracy and overfitting, DenseNet121 significantly improves stability, and the optimized ResNet50 achieves the best overall performance, standing out for its generalization capability and computational efficiency. These findings reinforce the effectiveness of combining transfer learning strategies with advanced training and preprocessing techniques in automatic facial emotion recognition. Keywords: Deep learning; Facial emotion recognition; CNN; DenseNet; ResNet; Transfer learning; Data augmentation; Image preprocessing.
evidence_items.title: Comparative Evaluation of CNN, DenseNet121, and Optimized ResNet50 for Facial Emotion Recognition on a Curated Dataset

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Adverse event (AE) reporting systems are central to hospital safety monitoring, yet severity classification remains dependent on human review and may be subject to variability among reviewers. Large language models (LLMs) may support more consistent classification of safety reports. Objective To evaluate agreement between a large language model (LLM)-based classification system and adjudicated expert human classifications of adverse event (AE) severity, while characterizing variability in the human classification process. Methods We analyzed 286 adverse event reports from the institutional safety reporting system of a tertiary academic medical center. Two quality and safety experts independently classified each report according to an A–I severity scale aligned with the National Coordinating Council for Medication Error Reporting and Prevention (NCC MERP) framework; disagreements were adjudicated by a third senior reviewer to establish the final human classification. The same reports were processed by a prespecified LLM-based workflow whose configuration was fixed before evaluation, without training, fine-tuning, calibration, or prompt modification on the study dataset; when the workflow generated clarification questions, the recorded responses were used to produce a second classification. Exact agreement with the final human classification was treated as the primary descriptive agreement measure; one-category differences and larger discordances were considered separately. Results Initial exact agreement between the two human reviewers was 65.4% (187/286), with moderate inter-rater reliability (unweighted Cohen’s κ = 0.563; linear weighted κ = 0.740). The final LLM classification exactly matched the final human classification in 140 of 286 cases (49.0%); 125 (43.7%) differed by one category within the prespecified A–E near-match range, and 21 (7.3%) were larger discordances. Linear weighted Cohen’s κ was 0.728 (bootstrap 95% CI, 0.678–0.770).
evidence_items.title: Large language model–based classification of adverse event severity: agreement with final human classification in a single-center study

evidence_items.summary: Background: Mendelian randomization (MR) has been widely used to investigate causal relationships between exposures and outcomes. However, concerns have also been raised about the reporting quality of MR studies. STROBE-MR was developed as a reporting guideline for MR studies, but assessments of compliance with STROBE-MR in published MR studies remain limited and rely largely on manual review. With the rapid development of large language models (LLMs), it is now possible to automate STROBE-MR compliance assessment. Methods: We developed a pipeline using OpenAI's GPT-5-mini model for automated assessment of MR reporting quality. Model performance was evaluated on an annotated dataset of 46 eligible MR articles. We applied the pipeline to more than 13,000 MR articles published between 2005 and 2025 to assess compliance with the STROBE-MR guideline and to explore reporting patterns across STROBE-MR items, sections, and time periods. Complete compliance required reporting all applicable components of an item; a sensitivity analysis used a partial compliance criterion requiring at least one applicable component. Results: Our LLM-based pipeline agreed with the human consensus on 89.0\% of the STROBE-MR assessments. On average, 22 of 43 items (51.2\%) met the complete compliance criterion, with substantial variation in reporting rates across STROBE-MR items and sections. The least reported items were found in the "Methods", "Results", and "Other Information" sections. The number of reported items remained stable over time, with slight decreases after 2021. Sensitivity analysis showed that temporal trend patterns differed between complete and partial compliance, particularly in the Methods, Discussion and Other Information sections. Conclusions: This study demonstrates the potential of LLMs to automate reporting quality assessment in MR studies.
evidence_items.title: Reporting Quality of Mendelian Randomization Studies Based on STROBE‑MR: An Investigation Powered by Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Evaluating long-horizon robot manipulation policies is a high-throughput computing workload: one CALVIN-style campaign sweeps checkpoints, seeds and task sequences across many concurrent simulator workers, consuming tens of thousands of rollouts before any score is inspected. Evaluation-path correctness is therefore a workflow-validation concern in parallel evaluation: an adapter defect shared by workers can yield a well-formed table of zeros while scheduler and determinism checks pass. We report a CALVIN case study and use it to propose the Benchmark-Fidelity Diagnostic Protocol (BFDP): a cheap-first set of single-worker controls, run before a parallel sweep, that audits export horizon, teacher replay semantics and reset fidelity in a fixed order. On Composing Actions from Language and Vision (CALVIN) scene D with a vision-language-to-diffusion pipeline, BFDP separates three findings of three different kinds. For the two tasks with a measured effect onset, the fixed 8-step export ends before the observed onset, and across benchmark-critical tasks it retains only 12–16% of the mean teacher-episode length. This is a confirmed defect of the export path: across all 14 episodes, in a paired intervention with export horizon as the only changed factor, exact-reset teacher replay rises from 0/14 to 14/14. The symbolic path returns one canonical robot state for all 64 probed initial conditions; this is the benchmark’s documented neutral reset rather than a defect, and the resulting exact-versus-symbolic split measures the sensitivity of our open-loop teacher control to its start state. Exact continuous replay reaches 1/3 on an official three-subtask probe, which bounds what teacher replay can establish under the official chained protocol rather than indicating a further defect. The full set of controls is between 0.36 and 1.8% of the subtask-rollout workload of the campaign it precedes, depending on how far the policy gets before each official sequence terminates.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark-path fidelity in parallel robot-policy evaluation: a CALVIN case study

evidence_items.summary: The Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index (EEXI), mandatory under MARPOL Annex VI since January 2023, requires existing ships to demonstrate a design-efficiency level that a large share of the conventionally configured fleet cannot meet without intervention. The tools available to evaluate and plan for compliance, however, are limited: certification grade calculators are proprietary and opaque, while academic treatments tend to embed the computation within one-off scenario studies rather than provide a reusable, openly described instrument. This paper presents the development and preliminary verification of an open, single-file, offline capable web based tool for EEXI calculation and compliance screening. The tool implements the attained-EEXI method of IMO Resolution MEPC.333(76) for the twelve applicable ship types, computes the required EEXI and a quantitative compliance verdict, models the engine and shaft power-limitation (EPL/ShaPoLi) regime, and estimates, for non-compliant vessels, the limiting rating that would bring the attained index to the required value. This was developed under the V-Model methodology, which embeds verification and validation as a structural counterpart of each design stage. Software verification and external validation are reported separately. For verification, two independently written implementations of the governing equations agreed to machine precision (ε ≤ 10⁻¹² %) across a thirteen-vessel matrix of hypothetical test cases spanning ship types, sizes, regulatory boundaries, and the power-limitation regime, and the inverse solver converged to the intended root; this establishes internal consistency of the encoding, not regulatory correctness. For external evidence, the outputs are compared with a published worked example (≈0.2 % deviation) and found to be consistent with an established commercial calculator and with the peer-reviewed literature.
evidence_items.title: An Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index (EEXI) calculation and compliance screening tool: Development, verification, and benchmark comparison

evidence_items.summary: Healthcare organizations generate large and diverse datasets through electronic health records, medical imaging, laboratory systems, wearable devices, claims, genomic studies, and public-health surveillance. Big Data Analytics (BDA) can transform these data into insights that support clinical decision-making, early risk identification, personalized care, resource planning, and population-health management. However, the value of analytics depends on data quality, interoperability, privacy, security, fairness, interpretability, and integration into clinical workflows. This paper presents a literature-based review of the role of BDA in healthcare and proposes a conceptual, end-to-end framework that connects data acquisition, governance, integration, scalable processing, analytical modelling, clinical validation, and responsible deployment. The discussion synthesizes findings reported in published reviews and highlights practical barriers that may prevent promising analytical models from producing measurable improvements in care. Rather than reporting a new clinical experiment, the paper develops a structured framework and a set of implementation recommendations for healthcare institutions. It concludes that BDA should be treated as a sociotechnical capability—not merely a software installation—with continuous monitoring, human oversight, and patient-centred governance as essential conditions for safe and sustainable adoption
evidence_items.title: Harnessing Big Data Analytics In Healthcare

Aourag). Main result: a three-filter screening (shear-modulus contrast, orientation-resolved coincidence-lattice matching, interfacial reactivity) of the 16 B2/C11b disilicide pairs. The most contrasted pairs (WSi2 or MoSi2 with AgY, MgY, AgSc or CoTi) react strongly with the disilicide and are rejected. Six aluminide pairs pass all filters; WSi2/NiAl and MoSi2/NiAl are proposed for a first experimental test of the Koehler contribution, with WSi2/CoAl as a weakly contrasted control. Compared for the same orientation and slip variant (resolved moduli and anisotropic Barnett–Lothe energy factors), the reactive pairs reach at most about 10% more maximum estimated image stress than the NiAl pairs, and the control has a 1.1–1.5 times smaller estimated image stress. 44-atom DFT superlattices (commensurate √5×√5/2×2 coincidence cells) give works of separation of 4.43–4.46 J/m² and interface energies of 2.14–2.21 J/m² for the NiAl pairs (2.15 J/m² for a second lateral registry of WSi2/NiAl), and 5.01 and 2.39 J/m² for the control. What is new in v3.0: WSi2/CoAl control superlattice (Quantum ESPRESSO input/output, CIF, interface energies); second lateral registry and k-point test of WSi2/NiAl; like-for-like image-stress estimates per slip variant (variants v3.py); resolved contrasts of CoTi, AgY and MgY (resolved others.py); {100}⟨001⟩ slip data; updated figures 6 and 7 with their scripts; complete archive of the Colab interface calculations (QE interfaces Colab.tar.gz); updated manifest.

evidence_items.summary: Machine-learning research on software vulnerability detection measures progress against a small set of public benchmark datasets, treated as a shared yardstick for comparing models. This approach rests on the untested premise that benchmarks agree: if two datasets have the same function, they give it the same label. We test this assumption by comparing four popular C and C++ benchmarks against one another on their complete data. Label agreement is a symmetric relation, but its strength is uneven. The two benchmarks that derive labels from CVE-linked fixing commits disagree on only 0.68% of 75,019 shared functions, whereas a third disagrees with them on 51.21% and 41.28%. Leakage, in contrast, is directed: we identify 1083 instances in which training data from one benchmark reappears in test data from another, with different counts in each direction. A manual check of 30 contradictory functions traces the disagreements to commit-level labeling and to treating functions left unchanged by a fix as safe. The costs are asymmetric: contradictory labels impair training only slightly, while up to 3.12% of a test set carries a contradicted label, shifting measured accuracy by up to two points. Therefore, reported accuracy reflects both model capabilities and benchmark selection.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Accuracy: A Cross-Benchmark Investigation of Label Consistency and Reliability in AI-Based Software Vulnerability Detection

evidence_items.summary: Geothermal resource development involves heterogeneous geological and engineering records, uncertain reservoir parameters, and decisions constrained by physical processes and safety requirements. This narrative and critical review examines how large language models (LLMs), including retrieval-augmented and tool-assisted systems, could support knowledge-intensive tasks throughout geothermal exploration, development, and operation. It distinguishes direct geothermal evidence from empirical evaluations in adjacent fields and from conceptual proposals; results from petroleum engineering, mineral exploration, and broader energy systems are not treated as proof of geothermal performance. Peer-reviewed studies demonstrate useful capabilities in technical document extraction, domain question answering, knowledge-graph reasoning, and interactions with scientific software, but direct geothermal engineering validation remains limited. For reservoir inversion, drilling-risk warning, and design optimization, quantitative assessment must rely on measured data and validated physical or numerical models, with LLMs acting as auditable interfaces and information-integration tools. The review proposes a task-specific benchmark framework and examines cross-domain transfer, multimodal alignment, knowledge-graph and retrieval collaboration, uncertainty quantification, and LLM–physical-model coupling. These frameworks are literature-informed proposals rather than implemented geothermal systems. Key priorities include independent geothermal test sets, expert-annotated reference answers, calibrated uncertainty, physics-based verification, and transparent reporting of model failure. The resulting synthesis identifies credible current applications and the evidence requirements for reliable future deployment.
evidence_items.title: From Data to Decision-Making: A Review of Large Language Model Applications Across the Full Lifecycle of Geothermal Resource Development

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Tables trapped in screenshots, scans, receipts and charts are usually extracted as markup that keeps the layout but not the relational meaning: merged cells stay merged, an invoice header and its line items stay unrelated, and “$1,250.00” stays a string. We study image-to-database reconstruction: given one image, produce a SQLite dump whose schema, column types, keys and rows load and can be queried as they are. Training data with exact gold databases is obtained in two ways: by rendering samples of the Spider databases at six layout levels, and by converting PubTabNet, FinTabNet and CORD annotations under the same normalization rules. A 2B model (Qwen3-VL-2B with LoRA) trained on 36,589 pairs and followed by a deterministic verify-and-repair layer reaches 0.86 table exact match and 0.99 foreign-key recall on rendered tables from unseen databases, against 0.75/0.75 for the 8B model of the same family prompted for SQL and 0.47/0.00 for an 8B HTML-to-SQLite pipeline. On held-out real images it obtains cell F1 0.81 (PubTabNet) and 0.96 (FinTabNet) and recall 0.93 on CORD receipt photos. On TabRecSet, a source not used in training, it is the best system that writes a database directly (0.52) but trails the 8B HTML pipeline (0.58), mostly in reading text from photographs. A variant trained on synthetic data alone matches the synthetic score and fails on real images, which locates the value of the real data. Code, model, data and all evaluation outputs are public.
evidence_items.title: PIX2DB: Reconstructing Executable Relational Databases from Document Images with a 2B Vision-Language Model

evidence_items.summary: Social media platforms often operate on extractive security logics that prioritize frictionless data sharing, leaving users disempowered and prone to oversharing sensitive information, without fully recognizing the associated privacy implications. We present WAIT-A-SEC (Warnings About Information Transfer And Sharing: Encouraging Caution), hereafter referred to as WAITASEC, an interactive proof-of-concept prototype that delivers real-time privacy alerts while users compose posts to minimize instances of oversharing. Leveraging a synthetic dataset of 90 annotated examples of realistic user-generated content, our evaluations compare three separate models 1) a rule-based regular expressions (regex) and named entity recognition (NER) through spaCy, 2) a large language model (LLM) and 3) a hybrid model that combines the previous two models as well as incorporates a knowledge graph (KG) and retrieval augmented generation (RAG) to provide context. In this hybrid approach, regex and NER yield candidate classifications, which are then validated and expanded by the LLM, utilizing RAG to retrieve relevant context from the KG before sending feedback back to the user. This classifier achieves optimal performance (Macro-F1 = 0.897; Micro-F1 = 0.834), significantly reducing critical false negatives. Grounded in Technical and Professional Communication (TPC) and active learning principles, we advocate for a warning-first design that introduces intentional pedagogical friction. This tactical approach promotes user reflection and fosters enduring privacy literacy, restoring user agency rather than relying on passive, automated redaction. This paper concludes with deployment considerations and next steps for user studies.
evidence_items.title: WAIT-A-SEC: A Human-Centered Design Approach to Privacy Communication for Social Media Oversharing

evidence_items.summary: Predicting the stopband width of finite one-dimensional dielectric Bragg reflectors requires a transfer-matrix calculation followed by spectrum-level edge extraction for each candidate stack. Although an individual wavelength-vectorized TMM evaluation is inexpensive, this calculation is repeated throughout large screening campaigns. Five supervised regressors are benchmarked as surrogates for the reflectance-defined stopband width ΔλStop of finite multilayers at normal incidence, in the lossless, non-dispersive limit. TMM spectra were generated for stacks parameterized by the refractive indices nL and nH, the layer thicknesses dL and dH, and the number of bilayers N. For each spectrum, ΔλStop was taken as the widest continuous interval with R(λ) ≥ 0.95. Designs with no such interval, or with a widest interval below 5 nm, were excluded, retaining 1660 of 2000 sampled designs. Hyperparameters of RF and SVR were selected by 10-fold cross-validation on the 1411-structure development set, while MLP depth was examined from one to ten hidden layers under the same test-isolated protocol. The selected six-hidden-layer MLP (128,64,32,16,16,16) achieved R2 = 0.9862, RMSE = 10.47 nm, and MAE = 5.92 nm on the independent 249-structure test set. On a structured external set of 120 quarter-wave designs from four dielectric pairs, the final MLP achieved R2 = 0.9688, RMSE = 5.67 nm, and MAE = 4.44 nm against the TMM reference; 94.17% of the cases had absolute errors below 10 nm and all 120 cases remained below 20 nm. Under an accuracy-controlled benchmark, the wavelength-vectorized TMM required 0.856 ms per structure at the selected 201-point spectral grid, whereas end-to-end single-sample inference with the final MLP, including input standardization, required 0.328 ms, corresponding to a 2.60× speedup. The surrogate is intended as a bounded-domain screening tool complementing, not replacing, full TMM analysis.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking machine-learning surrogates for rapid prediction of the reflectance-defined stopband width of finite dielectric Bragg reflectors

evidence_items.summary: DC-CoolTwin started as a workaround. We wanted to study how AI workloads, cooling water and cyberattacks affect each other in a data center, but there was no public dataset with all three on the same system. People usually use water-plant or industrial control data instead. We decided to simulate a data center ourselves. The dataset has four sites: Chittagong, Phoenix, Dublin and Singapore. Their climates are very different, which matters a lot for cooling water. Each site has 30 days of one-minute data (43,200 rows). Server load comes from real LLM traffic logs (BurstGPT, Azure 2024) and the weather is real too, from Open-Meteo. The simulator turns that into server heat, chiller and pump behavior, and cooling-tower water loss. We also attacked it. Seven attack types run for roughly 6% of the time: a fake temperature reading, a lowered set-point, replayed old data, a stuck water-level sensor, a drain valve forced open, and a network break-in that ends with tampered cooling settings. Besides 24 sensor columns and the attack labels, there's a column called water wasted L. It shows how much extra water each attack cost, compared with the same run without the attack. Water balance error is under 0.01%, and WUE stays between 1.77 and 2.55 L/kWh, close to real data centers. It should be useful for attack detection, adversarial testing, water forecasting, federated learning and cooling optimization. See README.txt for the columns.

evidence_items.summary: English proficiency prediction is an important task in vocational education because it is helpful in support teaching evaluation, personalized learning and early academic intervention. Traditional methods for predicting student performance mainly use structured educational properties such as test scores, classroom participation and attendance records. Although these methods can achieve certain prediction results, they often pay no attention to the semantic relationships contained in the students’ overall learning portfolios and have limited interpretability. To address this problem, this study proposes an interpretable large language model-based framework to predict English proficiency. Firstly, student learning records are transformed into natural language prompts, and semantic embeddings are learned using large language models. At the same time, structured educational features are standardized and encoded to build a structured representation. Then, a gated multimodal fusion module is designed to adaptively fuse semantic information and structured information. Finally, residual attention multi-layer perceptrons are used to classify the fused features to predict the students’ English proficiency. The experiment was carried out on a dataset of 200 student records from a vocational college for English learning. The results showed that the proposed model achieved an accuracy rate of 92.5% and a weighted F1 score of 91.3%, which is better than several traditional machine learning baseline models. Further analysis showed that the gated fusion mechanism could integrate semantic information and structured information. Feature importance analysis and case studies also shown that the proposed framework could provide interpretable prediction results and personalized learning recommendations.
evidence_items.title: Predicting English learning performance in vocational colleges using explainable large language models

evidence_items.summary: Language-model agents acquire capability along two routes that published work almost always varies together, one enlarging the computation a single agent performs and the other enlarging the number of agents and the channels along which they pass partial results, which leaves the contribution of each route indistinguishable. This paper separates an agent system into a reasoning operator and an interaction topology, holding the number of agents fixed at three across all multi-agent topologies, together with the number of rounds, the message cap, the prompt skeleton, and the memory settings for all combinations, and evaluates a full factorial design of four reasoning levels and four topologies on three public test sets totalling 484 instances under five random seeds, giving 38,720 task executions. Comparisons are paired at the instance level, and effects are estimated from logistic mixed-effects models fitted to each test set separately. The reasoning factor spans 18.0 points on the static suite whereas the topology factor spans 7.8 points on the interactive one, a reversal indicating that the two mechanisms act on different failure modes. The topology span is taken across all four topology levels and therefore includes the step from one agent to three, against a structure-only span of 2.8 points among the multi-agent topologies. The two factors also depart from additivity in a localised manner. A mechanism-motivated single-degree-of-freedom contrast on the only cell in which both factors contribute a corrective pass is significant at p = 0.001 on the static suite, whereas the omnibus nine-degree-of-freedom interaction test is not (p = 0.094), and in that cell the observed 50.0 percent lies 5.8 points below the additive expectation. After tokens are counted, seven of the sixteen configurations remain undominated on the static suite and five on the operating-system suite, and returns saturate at 12,400 tokens per instance on the static suite under the present design.
evidence_items.title: Autonomous Agents Based on Large Language Models: Reasoning Strategies and Multi-Agent Interaction
